name: Bushoong
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Vansina, J. 1959. Esquisse de Grammaire Bushong. Tervuren: Commission Linguistique Africaine (confirmed via Wikipedia Bushong stub; no digitized copy found)

new_statements.quote: The Bukuba language is quite free from a strong accent on any syllable, and, on the whole, is very smooth, rhythmical and musical. In simple words of two or three syllables there is a slight accent on the penult, with a secondary accent on fourth, fifth and sixth syllable in inflected words. Ano, he has died; alu, he rowed; amatawesha, he died for us; etc. Note 1. When the word has seven or eight syllables the primary accent falls on the antepenult and the secondary accent on the sixth syllable. Itashuhatashul'isha, he will save us.
new_statements.citation: Edmiston, Althea Brown. 1932. Grammar and dictionary of the Bushonga or Bukuba language as spoken by the Bushonga or Bukuba tribe who dwell in the Upper Kasai District, Belgian Congo, Central Africa. Luebo (Congo Belge): J. Leighton Wilson Press, American Presbyterian Congo Mission. viii+619 pp.
new_statements.locator: Part I (Orthography), section IV. ACCENT, para. 36 with Notes 1-2, pp. 13-14 (archive.org scan grammardictionar00edmi, PDF pages 25-26)
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent is weak; in simple words of two or three syllables it falls on the penultimate syllable; in long inflected (verb) forms of seven or eight syllables the primary accent shifts to the antepenult. The same source (Note 2, p. 14) reports that homographs accented on the same syllable are distinguished by a rising versus a falling 'inflection' on the accented syllable (shuoma 'swine' falling vs 'gift' rising; ngata 'woman' vs 'inside'; bata 'women' vs 'people'), i.e. lexical pitch/tone, and modern sources (Vansina 1959 data as reproduced in Grollemund et al. 2015 and Meeussen 1962/2014; Hulstaert 1985) treat Bushong as a tone language with H/L tones. So: tonal language, with a 1932 statement of weak penultimate accent.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Stated: 'a secondary accent on fourth, fifth and sixth syllable in inflected words' (direction of counting not made explicit); in seven- or eight-syllable words the secondary accent is on the sixth syllable (Note 1).
new_statements.exceptions: Words of seven or eight syllables take primary accent on the antepenult instead of the penult (Note 1). Diphthongs count as syllables (Rem.: buala 'disease', muana 'child', mvedi 'star'). Note 2 reports rising vs falling pitch on the accented syllable distinguishing otherwise identical words.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, including inflected verb forms (examples are verb forms and nouns in isolation); no phrase-level statement except p. ~ para. 416 that yes/no questions are marked by a raised tone of voice on the last vowel of the sentence. Impressionistic missionary description from 1932; no tone marking in the grammar or dictionary.
new_statements.identity_note: Edmiston's "Bushonga or Bukuba language... of the Upper Kasai District" is the central Kuba-kingdom dialect (Bushoong proper, bush1247; Glottolog alternate names Bushongo, Kuba, Shongo). She notes (p. 2) that subject groups (Bapianga, Bangende, Bashoba, Bakele) speak it "with certain variations in accent and pronunciation called by the Bakuba the Lumbila". Glottolog lists Edmiston twice (1932 'grammar' and '1940' grammar_sketch, viii+619 pp.): the archive.org scan (viii, 619 p., dated 1932) shows these are one and the same book. Denolf 1932 describes the Mpianga (Lupianga) dialect, a different Kuba variety.
